records.name_note: The two admissible sources with dedicated pages for this exact species spell the name two ways. NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list (alphabetized) reads Paper Bark Maple, Paperbark Maple, and its Description prose opens 'Paperbark maple, a small, woody, deciduous tree in the maple family (Sapindaceae), originates from Central China.' RHS's plant profile shows paperbark maple as the common-name subtitle under its H1 Acer griseum. The one-word spelling Paperbark Maple is the NC State prose lead and the RHS subtitle, so it is used as the common name. Distinct from Acer palmatum (Japanese Maple), Acer rubrum (Red Maple) and Acer pensylvanicum (Moosewood) already in this catalog.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: NC State's Acer griseum page carries no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags, and RHS's page has no toxicity statement. The red-maple horse-leaf warning belongs to A. rubrum and was not extended to this species.

MoBot (plantfinder.mobot.org / www.missouribotanicalgarden.org) could not be loaded in this session: every fetch returned a connect error, and curl failed on an SSL certificate error. No MoBot data is used, and I did not try to work around the error. Clemson, UF/IFAS, PSU, UMD and UGA were not found to have a dedicated Acer griseum page and were not used.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0) together, so the bands are open-ended. RHS also lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral'.

water_regime left null: neither source has a watering statement. NC State's description says 'moist, well-drained soil' (a soil adjective). RHS's structured Moisture field reads 'Moist but well-drained or Well-drained', which is mixed and does not support a single regime. water_dry_down_target and the day-interval fields are null because this is an in-ground tree and no source frames watering that way.

soil_drainage moderate rests on NC State's Good Drainage + Moist tag pair and its 'moist, well-drained soil' prose. RHS's Cultivation line, 'Grow in a moist but well-drained soil', agrees, but it may be shared genus-level text and is not relied on.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's Light field lists Full sun and Partial Shade (2-6 hours of direct sun), and RHS's Position field lists Full sun and Partial shade. The Partial Shade tag is mapped to part_shade. direct_sun_hours_max is null because the only hour range on the page comes from the generic NC State light legend, not species prose.

Temperatures, humidity, indoor light, chill damage and fertilizing are null because no admissible source states them. NC State and RHS give only hardiness ratings (NC State zones 4a-8b, RHS hardiness rating H5), which are not damage-onset temperatures.
is_edible is null: no source addresses eating this plant. The NC State 'Wildlife Food Source' play-value tag and the Songbirds attractant refer to wildlife, not human food.
is_houseplant is false based on both sources describing a landscape tree (NC State: 'small, woody, deciduous tree'; Plant Type Tree). Neither source discusses indoor culture.

Size: NC State's own Dimensions block is the anchor (Height 20-30 ft = 240-360 in; Width 15-25 ft = 180-300 in). RHS gives larger Max Height 8-12 m (315-472 in) and Max Spread 4-8 m (157-315 in) over 20-50 years to maturity. The two sources disagree on height, and the NC State figures were used.
attracts_pollinators is true from NC State's Attracts field (Moths, Pollinators, Songbirds) and its Play Value tag 'Attracts Pollinators'. RHS carries no pollinator tag.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page for Forsythia suspensa carries no Poison block and no handling warning. Its Tags list reads, in full: "#deciduous #children's garden #cozy #winter flowers #non-toxic for cats #non-toxic for horses #non-toxic for dogs #playground plant #perennial #pruning tolerant #deciduous shrub #yellow flowers #shrub #flowering shrub". The non-toxic for cats and non-toxic for dogs tags are what support toxic_to_pets=false (the horses tag is a different animal). No admissible source reviewed addresses toxicity to people, which parts are involved, or fruit use; the fruit's traditional-medicine use (lian qiao) is not an edibility statement and no admissible source was found for it. The MoBot species page could not be loaded, so it was not compared.
unknowns: name_note left null: NC State and RHS both lead with Weeping Forsythia / weeping forsythia for this exact taxon, so no split. NC State's structured module lists Forsythia x intermedia as often confused with this species; nothing on this page supplies any field for the hybrid, and none was borrowed.

MoBot Plant Finder species page (taxonid 282935) could not be loaded: the host plantfinder.mobot.org refused the connection through the sandbox proxy, so no MoBot evidence was used. Clemson HGIC returned 403 for the factsheet, and ask.ifas.ufl.edu was not reachable; no species-specific page from UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD or UGA was found.

is_houseplant false: NC State's Landscape Location lists Lawn and Recreational Play Area (no Houseplants or Container entry) over USDA zones 5a-8b, and RHS describes a deciduous arching shrub to 3m; no admissible source says anything about indoor culture.

toxic_to_pets=false rests only on NC State's non-toxic for cats and non-toxic for dogs tags; there is no Poison block, so no human toxicity or poison-part information. RHS has no toxicity field. is_edible null: no admissible source states food use or inedibility (lian qiao use of the fruit in traditional Chinese medicine is not an edibility statement).

RHS lists Max Height 2.5-4 metres and Max Spread 2.5-4 metres (98.4-157.5 inches) with a 5-10 year time to maturity; NC State's own species Dimensions (8-10 ft tall, 6-10 ft wide) were used as the anchor, and RHS is higher at the top end.

outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun only: RHS's Position field lists Full sun only and its species Cultivation text reads 'Grows best in moist but well-drained soil in full sun'; NC State's Light field lists Dappled Sunlight, Full sun, and Partial Shade, and its prose says 'full sun to shade', a tolerance statement. Per the RHS-Position precedent, part_shade and full_shade were not added.
soil_ph_min/max null: NC State carries no pH field and RHS lists pH as Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, which sets no bound.

Watering: NC State prose says 'medium moisture, well-drained soils' which is a soil description, not a watering instruction; water_regime and all interval fields left null. Humidity, temperature, chill damage, light in foot-candles, fertilizing, and direct-sun hours have no admissible species-specific source.
attracts_pollinators null: NC State has no Attracts field and RHS has no attractive-to-pollinators tag on this page.

soil_base garden_bed is an in-ground classification inferred from the shrub being described as a garden/landscape plant tolerating 'average to poor garden soils', not from an explicit soil-mix statement.
NC State previously-known-as synonyms: Forsythia fortunei, Forsythia sieboldii, Forsythia suspensa var. pubescens, Forsythia suspensa var. sieboldii; RHS lists the name status as Correct.

records.name_note: NC State's Common Name(s) list gives Coral Yucca first, then Hummingbird Yucca, Redflower False Yucca, Red Yucca and Yellow Yucca. Its Description prose calls the plant 'Red yucca' ('Red yucca is a member of the asparagus family (Asparagaceae)'). RHS's subtitle under the H1 is 'small-flowered hesperaloe', and RHS lists Aloe yuccifolia as a synonym. Red Yucca is used as common_name on NC State's Description prose opener, which is not what its list leads with: it is a deliberate choice, and Coral Yucca, the list's first entry, is recorded here as the alternative. MoBot's page could not be loaded, so its name was not compared. Hesperaloe is not a true Yucca (nor an Aloe); distinct from Yucca filamentosa (Adam's Needle) and Yucca gigantea (Yucca Cane) already in this catalog, and from Yucca gloriosa (Spanish Dagger) in this batch.
unknowns: MoBot Plant Finder (plantfinder.mobot.org taxonid=281957) could not be loaded: TLS certificate verification failed (unable to verify the first certificate) from both the cache fetcher and curl, so no MoBot content was used and the common-name comparison with MoBot is missing.
No UF/IFAS, Clemson, Penn State, UMD or UGA page dedicated to Hesperaloe parviflora was found; Clemson hits were multi-species factsheets and were not used.
toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null: no admissible source reviewed states pet toxicity or safety. No yucca saponin toxicity was borrowed. Name trap: it is not a true Yucca or an Aloe.

is_houseplant false: NC State's Landscape Location lists Coastal and Container (no Houseplants entry) over USDA zones 6a-10b and says 'It can also be planted in large containers', which is outdoor container use; no source frames it as a houseplant.
is_edible null: no admissible source addresses eating.

water_regime, water_dry_down_target and the watering-day fields are null: NC State gives no watering instruction, only drought and dry-soil tolerance tags. RHS's watering and fertiliser advice applies only 'Under glass' and is conditional, so it was not used.
fertilize fields null for the same reason: the only RHS fertiliser statement is under glass.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max null: RHS gives only the qualitative 'Acid or Neutral' and NC State gives no pH field.
chill_damage_f null: NC State lists USDA zones 6a-10b and RHS gives H4; these are hardiness ratings, not damage-onset temperatures.
Temperature, humidity, light_fc and direct_sun_hours_max null: no species-specific admissible figure. NC State's '6 or more hours' sits in the site-wide light legend.

soil_drainage fast rests on NC State: sandy, 'Superior soil drainage is essential', root rot in damp heavy soils, and Occasionally Dry and Very Dry tags with no wet tolerance. RHS's 'sharply-drained' wording is in a Cultivation paragraph that may be genus boilerplate, so it was not cited.

outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun only. NC State's Light field also lists Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours), but RHS's structured Position lists Full sun only and NC State's prose says 'in full sun', so part_shade was dropped. MoBot could not be loaded.
soil_base garden_bed is an in-ground reading from NC State's soil description. NC State also says the plant can be planted in large containers.

mature size from NC State's Dimensions block (Height 3-5 ft = 36-60 in; Width 4-6 ft = 48-72 in). RHS's Max Height of 1-1.5 metres (39.4-59.1 in) agrees; its Max Spread of 0.1-0.5 metres (4-20 in) is far narrower than NC State's width and looks anomalous, so NC State was used.
RHS lists the Name Status as Correct and 'Aloe yuccifolia' as a synonym.

records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name. NC State's dedicated Yucca gloriosa page leads its Common Name(s) list with Mound Lily Yucca (then Spanish Dagger, Spanish Dagger Yucca), and its description opens 'Mound lily yucca is an evergreen perennial...'. RHS's dedicated page shows the heading Yucca gloriosa with the common-name subtitle Spanish dagger, and carries a separate 'Other common names' list (Adam's needle, Lord's candlestick, mound lily, palm lily, Roman candle, tree lily). UF/IFAS FP616 lists 'Spanish dagger, moundlily yucca' with Spanish dagger first. Spanish Dagger is therefore used because two of the three admissible sources (RHS, UF/IFAS) lead with it. UF/IFAS says Spanish dagger is often confused with Spanish bayonet (Yucca aloifolia). NC State lists var. tristis under this species' Cultivars / Varieties, and RHS has a separate Yucca gloriosa var. tristis page that lists Yucca recurva as a synonym. RHS's 'Adam's needle' is the name this catalog already lands for Yucca filamentosa, a different species, so it is not used here; distinct also from Yucca gigantea (Yucca Cane) and from Hesperaloe parviflora (Red Yucca) in this batch.
records.toxicity_detail: Pet scope: RHS's dedicated Yucca gloriosa page, 'Potentially harmful' field, reads in full: 'Skin allergen. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling' and 'Pets (dogs, cats): Harmful if eaten - for further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants', so both dogs and cats are named and the handling warning is to wear gloves and other protective equipment. RHS gives no symptom list, no poison-part list and no severity rating. NC State's Problems field on the same species lists Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs and Problem for Horses (also carried as the tags #problem for dogs, #problem for horses, #problem for cats); the NC State page has no Poison block, no symptom list, no poison-part list and no severity rating, and these entries are not a severity rating. Sharp leaf tips: NC State describes 'sharp-tipped leaves' and lists Appendage: Spines; RHS describes 'spine-tipped, stiff, glaucous-green leaves'; UF/IFAS says 'With the sharp needled tips removed with shears, Spanish dagger makes a wonderful accent at entryways or in a shrub border'. Edibility versus harm: NC State's Edibility field says 'Flowers, fruits, roots, and stems are edible. Flowers are tasty raw or cooked, and the stems can be used like asparagus. The roots can be cooked or dried and ground into a powder that can be used to make bread'; UF/IFAS lists the fruit characteristic as 'suited for human consumption'. RHS, by contrast, flags it harmful if eaten by dogs and cats and a skin allergen. The admissible sources therefore differ on eating, and NC State's edibility text carries no stated risk to people or pets. No admissible source mentions saponins.
unknowns: Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder returns only the cultivar page Yucca gloriosa 'Variegata' (Spanish dagger) for this name, with no dedicated species page, so MoBot was not used. No Clemson, Penn State or UMD page for this exact species was found.

No admissible source mentions saponins, so no saponin pet-toxicity claim is made. Pet toxicity rests on RHS's 'Pets (dogs, cats): Harmful if eaten' and NC State's Problem for Cats/Dogs/Horses tags. Neither gives symptoms, a poison part or a severity rating.

is_houseplant false: NC State's Landscape Location lists Coastal, Container and Naturalized Area (no Houseplants entry) over USDA zones 7a-11b, NC State's Dimensions give 6-16 ft, and UF/IFAS (zones 6-11) and RHS (H5) treat it as an outdoor landscape shrub. The research record set true on NC State's single sentence 'Mound lily yucca is often used as a container plant and can be grown as a house plant.'; that sentence is kept as a disclosed counterpoint. No admissible source gives indoor light, temperature, humidity or watering guidance, so all indoor-care fields are null.

Edibility: NC State says flowers, fruits, roots and stems are edible and UF/IFAS says the fruit is suited for human consumption, while RHS says the plant is harmful if eaten by dogs and cats and is a skin allergen. is_edible is true only for the parts and preparations NC State describes. Do not read it as safe for pets.

soil_drainage left null. NC State's Soil Drainage tags are Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry and Very Dry (no wet tag) and its prose prefers well-drained sandy soils. RHS and UF/IFAS say only well-drained, which is ambiguous on its own.

water_regime dry_thoroughly_between is an interpretation of UF/IFAS's species-page sentence that it 'should be watered sparingly, if at all'. NC State has no watering statement, and its Moist drainage tag is a soil descriptor, not a watering instruction. RHS's cultivation paragraph is genus boilerplate shared with Yucca filamentosa and was not used. water_dry_down_target and the day-interval fields are null because this is an in-ground shrub and no source frames watering that way.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light field gives full sun plus Partial Shade (2-6 hours of direct sun), mapped to part_shade; RHS's Position field says full sun and UF/IFAS says part shade/part sun. part_sun was not added, to avoid going brighter than NC State's partial shade. direct_sun_hours_max is null because only NC State's generic light legend gives hour ranges.
Soil pH null: RHS says 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' (no bounds) and UF/IFAS lists alkaline and acidic soil tolerances, so no ceiling or floor can be set.

Size sources differ. mature_height_in and mature_spread_in follow NC State's Dimensions block (Height 6-16 ft = 72-192 in; Width 6-8 ft = 72-96 in). UF/IFAS gives height 6 to 8 feet and spread 4 to 8 feet, and RHS gives 1.5-2.5 metres (59.1-98.4 in) for both max height and max spread.

chill_damage_f is null: NC State's USDA zones 7a-11b, UF/IFAS zones 6-11 and RHS H5 are hardiness ratings, not a damage-onset temperature. Humidity, fertilizer, day and night temperature and light footcandle fields have no admissible species-specific source and are null.

Taxonomy: NC State lists var. tristis under Yucca gloriosa's cultivars/varieties and RHS has a separate var. tristis page with synonym Yucca recurva. No admissible source examined here states that Yucca recurvifolia is treated as var. tristis. RHS also lists a Yucca gloriosa var. recurvifolia 'Mellow Yellow' cultivar page.
Related species are not merged into this record. Yucca aloifolia (Spanish bayonet) is a different taxon that is confusable with this one. Yucca filamentosa and Yucca gigantea are landed separately.

records.name_note: Sources lead with slightly different names. NC State's Common Name(s) list (alphabetized) begins with Cuckoo Pint and also includes Italian Arum. The RHS dedicated page's H1 is Arum italicum and its plant-profile common-name subtitle is Italian arum; RHS gives Italian lords-and-ladies under a separate Other common names heading. The Penn State Extension page leads with Italian Lords and Ladies and says it is also called Italian Arum. Italian Arum was chosen because it is the RHS common-name subtitle and both NC State and Penn State list it. NC State's "often confused with" module for this page lists Arum maculatum (with Dracunculus vulgaris and Zantedeschia aethiopica).
records.toxicity_detail: NC State (Poisonous to Humans block, human-scoped): Poison Severity High; Poison Symptoms: "Ingesting any part of this plant may lead to symptoms of throat and tongue swelling. This may cause increased difficulty breathing and result in possible death. Physical contact with this plant can cause skin irritation."; Poison Toxic Principle: Calcium oxalate crystals; Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes; Poison Part: Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Seeds, Stems (full list as rendered). NC State's separate Problems tag list (distinct from the Poison block) reads Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses, Weedy; the cat and dog tags are the basis for toxic_to_pets=true. NC State Plant Type values: Bulb, Herbaceous Perennial, Poisonous. Handling warning (NC State): "Be sure to wear gloves and protective clothing when handling this plant. All the plant parts can cause skin irritation." RHS: "TOXIC if eaten; skin/eye irritant. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling" (RHS's separate "TOXIC to pets" line names no animal, so it was not used for toxic_to_pets). Penn State Extension Master Gardener page: "All parts of this plant are toxic, so keep young children away from it." Fruits (the orangish-red berries) are one of the listed poison parts, but no admissible page that could be read states that the berries are the main ingestion risk; NC State lists all parts. No admissible page read mentions the sap separately; the skin-irritation warnings cover all plant parts. Sources do not disagree on scope (no fruit-only reading) or on edibility; none says any part is eaten.
unknowns: Missouri Botanical Garden (www.missouribotanicalgarden.org / plantfinder.mobot.org, kempercode=y760) could not be fetched in this session (ConnectError even with the hosts allowed), so no MoBot content is used. It was not read for common name, sun, water, size or toxicity.

Invasive status by state: no admissible page read gives a state-by-state invasive list. NC State says 'It is considered invasive in some parts of the United States because it is difficult to control and spreads rapidly' and 'The species is invasive on the West Coast and the Mid-Atlantic United States', lists it as introduced in DC, IL, MD, MO, NY, NC, OR, WA, and notes the NC Native Plant Society Watch List Class A placement in 2010. As an alternative to garden planting where it may be invasive, NC State suggests: 'Alternatively, keep the plant confined in a container and remove fruits before they are ripe.' Penn State says it has become invasive in places like the Pacific Northwest. The UMD IPMnet weed index lists Arum, Italian (Arum italicum) as a weed (report 24Mar22), with no state-level invasive designation read.

toxic_to_pets is true on NC State's Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags only. RHS's 'TOXIC to pets' line names no animal and was not used. NC State's severity rating (High) comes from its Poisonous to Humans block and is human-scoped.

is_houseplant=true rests on NC State's Landscape Location list (Container, Houseplants, Naturalized Area, Woodland) and Penn State's statement that it can be grown as a houseplant; the plant is mainly a hardy garden perennial that goes dormant in summer.

outdoor_sun_exposure is part_shade only. NC State's structured Light field lists Deep shade and Partial Shade (2-6 hours); RHS's structured Position lists Full sun and Partial shade. full_sun is left out because NC State's structured Light field excludes it (its prose 'grows in partial shade to full sun' is a tolerance statement), and full_shade is left out for the mirror-image reason: RHS's structured Position excludes it, and it otherwise rests on NC State's Deep shade value, its Resistance To Challenges 'Heavy Shade', and Penn State's 'Arum italicum grows well in shady or partial sun and has been recommended as a good choice for growing among hostas.' MoBot could not be checked as a tiebreaker.
direct_sun_hours_max left null: no species-specific prose gives an hour figure (NC State's 2-6 hours for Partial Shade is the site-wide category definition).
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), which are open-ended bands, and RHS lists Acid or Alkaline or Neutral.

water_regime left null: pages give only soil adjectives (moist, humus-rich, well-drained) and no watering instruction; water_dry_down_target and day-interval fields left null for an in-ground perennial. NC State's tags also include Resistance To Challenges: Wet Soil, and Penn State says it is more tolerant of standing water than most garden plants. RHS's cultivation sentence may be genus-level boilerplate and was not used for soil_drainage.
soil_base=garden_bed is a categorisation for an in-ground, humus-rich-soil perennial, not a stated potting mix; no potting recommendation is given by any source read.

Size: NC State Dimensions give Height 1 ft 0 in - 2 ft 0 in and Width 1 ft 0 in - 2 ft 0 in (12-24 in each). Its description prose says 'up to 12 to 18 inches tall' and RHS Max Height and Max Spread are 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in); the structured NC State dimensions were used.
is_edible=false rests on RHS 'TOXIC if eaten'; NC State carries the #poisonous if ingested tag. No source describes any part as food.

attracts_pollinators=true rests on NC State's statement that small flies pollinate the flowers; NC State's own Attracts field is not present on this page, and no bees/butterflies/hummingbirds are named.

Temperature, humidity, light in foot-candles, fertilizer and chill-damage fields have no admissible-source support and are left null. NC State hardiness zones 5a-9b and RHS H6 are growing-range ratings, not damage-onset temperatures.

Name trap: Arum maculatum also goes by Cuckoo Pint and Lords and Ladies, and NC State lists Cuckoo Pint and Lords and Ladies for Arum italicum too; these shared names do not identify the species. Only the dedicated Arum italicum pages of NC State and RHS, and the Penn State Extension Warren County Italian Lords and Ladies page, were used, never Marmoratum or other cultivar pages.

normalizations: 2026-10-09: b134 (mixed gaps) landed from the post-audit records with b134_repair.py.
